name: Oseltamivir
mechanism: Prodrug converted to active oseltamivir carboxylate, which competitively inhibits influenza viral neuraminidase (both A and B). Prevents viral release from infected cells and spread to new cells. Reduces viral shedding, symptom duration (~1 day if started early), and complications
dosing: Treatment: 75mg PO BD for 5 days (start within 48h of symptoms for greatest benefit, but may benefit even if >48h in severe illness). Prophylaxis: 75mg PO OD for 10 days (post-exposure) or throughout influenza season (seasonal). Severe illness/immunocompromised: consider higher dose (150mg BD) or longer duration (specialist advice). Reduce in renal impairment: CrCl 30-60: 30mg BD (treatment), 30mg OD (prophylaxis); CrCl 10-30: 30mg OD (treatment), 30mg alternate days (prophylaxis). Paediatric dosing weight-based
contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Severe renal impairment (CrCl <10) - dose data limited. Not a substitute for influenza vaccination
interactions: Minimal interactions. Competes with probenecid (renal tubular secretion). Live attenuated influenza vaccine: oseltamivir may reduce vaccine efficacy (avoid oseltamivir 48h before to 2 weeks after vaccine). No significant CYP interactions
monitoring: Clinical response (symptom duration, fever resolution). Signs of secondary bacterial infection (persistent/worsening symptoms). Renal function (dose adjustment). Neuropsychiatric symptoms (rare, especially children/adolescents - confusion, abnormal behaviour)
pregnancy: Benefits likely outweigh risks. Influenza in pregnancy higher risk of complications. Use if clinically indicated (treatment or prophylaxis). Some data suggests safety. WHO/CDC recommend use in pregnancy
sideEffects: Common: nausea, vomiting (10-15%, less if taken with food), abdominal pain, headache, fatigue. Uncommon: diarrhoea, dizziness. Rare: neuropsychiatric events (confusion, delirium, abnormal behaviour, hallucinations - mainly in children/adolescents, especially Japan. Causality uncertain - may be influenza itself). Hypersensitivity reactions (rash, anaphylaxis - rare), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (very rare), hepatitis (rare)
pharmacokinetics: Oral prodrug. Rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by hepatic esterases to active oseltamivir carboxylate. Bioavailability >75%. Peak active drug: 2-3h. Minimal protein binding (<3%). Not significantly metabolized by CYP. Half-life: 6-10h (active metabolite). Excreted renally (>90% as active metabolite) - dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Food improves tolerability (no significant effect on absorption)
clinicalPearls: Brand: Tamiflu. Widely stockpiled for influenza pandemics. EFFECTIVENESS: reduces symptom duration by ~1 day if started within 48h of onset. May reduce complications (pneumonia, hospitalization) especially in high-risk groups (elderly, immunocompromised, pregnant, chronic disease). Benefit after 48h controversial for uncomplicated influenza, but consider in severe/high-risk. INDICATIONS: treatment of influenza A/B (ideally within 48h). Prophylaxis: post-exposure (household contact), seasonal (institutional outbreaks, unvaccinated high-risk). NOT first-line prevention - vaccination superior. Use prophylaxis in unvaccinated exposed high-risk individuals. RESISTANCE: rare but described (H275Y mutation in N1 - oseltamivir-resistant, zanamivir-sensitive). More common in immunocompromised on prolonged treatment. START EARLY: benefit greatest if within 48h. In severe illness/hospitalization, start empirically even if >48h (may still benefit). Take with food to reduce nausea. Not effective against bacterial complications (secondary pneumonia) - if suspected, add antibiotics. Neuropsychiatric events: mainly children/adolescents, especially in Japan (reports of abnormal behaviour, falls, self-injury). Causality unclear - influenza itself causes delirium. Monitor, counsel parents. Alternative: zanamivir (inhaled, less GI side effects, but poor in asthma/COPD - bronchospasm risk). NEW agents: baloxavir (single-dose, alternative mechanism - cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor). Consider oseltamivir in: severe influenza requiring hospitalization, high-risk groups (pregnancy, immunocompromised, chronic lung/heart disease, >65 years), care home outbreaks. Not needed for healthy young adults with mild illness
indication: Treatment of influenza A and B (ideally within 48h of symptom onset). Post-exposure prophylaxis and seasonal prophylaxis of influenza in at-risk individuals
